text:
In late October 2024, Alexei Bolgov, a sergeant guarding a military headquarters in the occupied Donetsk region, told his wife, Natalya, over the phone: “It’s horrific, what’s going on here. I’ll tell you when I get back.”
He never made it home. Five weeks later, shortly after turning 29, Bolgov walked about 300 metres from his unit’s command post near the village of Stepove into woodland and shot himself, according to a written account by his commander seen by the Guardian.
“On the day of his death, Bolgov was in a withdrawn state,” his commander wrote.
Bolgov is one of more than 1,000 Russian soldiers recorded as having died by suicide since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, according to confidential data from Russia’s state statistics agency, Rosstat, analysed by the Guardian.
The deaths of a further 885 soldiers in or near Ukraine were recorded as firearm-related injuries of “undetermined intent”, a classification that experts say can conceal suicides and that was used in several cases independently identified by the Guardian as suicides.
Taken together, the suicides amount to approximately a Russian regiment of dead.
The data, which analysts say almost certainly underestimates the true number of suicides, offers a rare, previously unreported glimpse of the strain on Russia’s armed forces nearly five years into a war in which heavy losses and harsh discipline have sapped morale.
Suicides among soldiers are a feature of most wars. A New York Times investigation found that at least 158 active-duty US army soldiers died by suicide in 2023.
But in Russia’s army, military analysts say, the problem is compounded by intense pressure from fellow soldiers and commanders, as well as fear of being sent on extremely dangerous combat missions. Contracts that in effect leave soldiers with no way out of the war add to the sense of desperation.
“There’s clearly a lot of coercion used by the Russian military to force people to go forward. In some cases, they will abuse them, torture them, use different types of physical abuse,” said Rob Lee, a senior fellow at the Foreign Policy Research Institute. “So it’s not surprising that some guys commit suicide,” he added.
The figures come from a cache of more than 11m death certificates obtained by the Belarusian opposition-linked hacking group Cyber Partisans and the Ukrainian hacker collective Silent Crow.
The Kremlin does not publish data on suicides in the military and treats casualty figures as a state secret.
Of the 1,087 suicides by military personnel identified by the Guardian, at least 614 took place in occupied areas of Ukraine or Russian regions bordering it, mainly Belgorod and Bryansk. A further 113 records did not specify a location of death.
More than half of suicides involved firearms – particularly those near the frontlines. The deaths occurred at military camps, combat positions, training grounds and private homes.
Of those suicides that took place in the war zone, 43 were young soldiers aged 18 or 19.
The figures also include 108 men under 25 who died by suicide elsewhere in Russia away from the front. Some are likely to have been conscripts, who are not formally sent to fight in Ukraine but have often been pressed to sign contracts that allow them to be deployed.
Recorded military suicides have risen as the war has gone on, from more than 50 in 2022 to more than 200 in 2024, peaking at 365 in 2025 – mirroring Russia’s overall death toll. In 2026 – despite records being incomplete and lagging behind the battlefield reality – the database already records almost 300 suicides, the second highest total for any year of the war so far.
Activists and lawyers who work with Russian deserters believe the real number is higher.
“I would say it is a low estimate,” said Ivan Chuvilyaev, a spokesperson for Idite Lesom, a group that helps Russian soldiers desert. “Obviously, it is a lot more.”
He described the frontline as “a tin can” from which little information escapes. “Any Rosstat statistic, like any statistic relating to the war, is just reports passed up the chain.
“A man can kill himself, and on paper he is a hero. His parents might even be sent some medal,” Chuvilyaev said.
Officials, he added, had little interest in an accurate count, as the figures would be scrutinised further up the chain of command.
Chuvilyaev and Lee also suggested that most cases in which Russian soldiers took their own lives on the battlefield, often after being wounded or as a Ukrainian drone approached, would probably be recorded as combat deaths rather than suicides. Such incidents have been documented in numerous grim videos from the front.
The gaps are visible in the Rosstat data.
Sergei Savenok, a 62-year-old lieutenant colonel from the Irkutsk region, volunteered in September 2022. Before leaving for the front, he is seen in a video clip taking to the stage of his local community centre to address the men heading off with him. “I’m from Donbas myself. Let’s fucking smash them, lads! That’s all!” he shouted, to applause.
He was found shot dead in occupied Luhansk region in July 2023. His wife, Yelena was informed by officials that his death was suicide, but he does not appear among the suicides in the Rosstat records.
A certificate matching his date of birth instead records a death from injury resulting from the discharge of a handheld firearm, with undetermined intent.
The Guardian was able to identify 1,038 military related deaths with similar causes – 885 of which took place in Ukraine or a bordering region of Russia.
Nor does Alexander Lazor, a 21-year-old private who died near the village of Solodke in Donetsk region in the summer of 2022, appear among the suicides in the records.
His family was told he was killed in combat, and in Rosstat data he is listed to have succumbed to “injuries due to warfare caused by firearms”.
But two soldiers who served alongside Lazor told the Guardian that members of their unit had been informed he had taken his own life.
“Our whole unit was told he killed himself. Perhaps, they decided to cover it up so that our unit doesn’t look bad,” said one of the soldiers, who spoke on condition of anonymity, speculating about why his comrade’s death had not been officially recorded as a suicide.
The suicides are just one sign of an army under strain.
By the end of May 2025, Russian military courts had received cases against 20,662 men for refusing to serve, most for going absent without leave, according to the independent outlet Mediazona. IStories verified this data and found at least 49,000 servicemen of the Russian armed forces had been declared deserters or Awol.
Thoughts of suicide were common among the soldiers Idite Lesom helped to desert, Chuvilyaev said.
“Of course they appear,” he said. “It’s the next stop, after a man realises where he has ended up.”
